name: Broccoli
description: A cool-season crop that produces a large central head, followed by smaller side shoots after the main harvest.
tips: For a fall harvest, start seeds indoors in mid-summer. Plant when soil temperature is consistently between 60-75°F. Heat can cause premature flowering (bolting).
succession: For a continuous harvest, plant new seedlings every 2-3 weeks.
yield: 1 large central head and multiple smaller side shoots per plant.
harvestInstructions: Harvest the main head when it is firm and tight, before the flower buds open. Cut the stalk at an angle. The plant will continue to produce smaller side shoots for a prolonged harvest.
containerGardening: Possible in large (5+ gallon) pots. Requires consistent watering and feeding to form a good head.

soil.notes: Prefers soil rich in organic matter. Add compost before planting.

temperature.notes: Growth slows and flavor can become bitter in temperatures above 80°F.

environmentalAlerts.message: Broccoli is frost tolerant, but cover if a hard freeze is expected to protect developing heads.

storage: Store unwashed in a perforated plastic bag in the crisper drawer for up to a week. For long-term preservation, blanch florets and freeze.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over 7-10 days to prevent transplant shock.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply a 2-3 inch layer of organic mulch (like straw or shredded leaves) to retain soil moisture, regulate soil temperature, and suppress weeds.

careTasks.name: Fertilize with nitrogen
careTasks.description: Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer (e.g., blood meal or a balanced liquid fertilizer) to encourage vigorous leaf growth.

careTasks.name: Monitor for cabbage worms and aphids
careTasks.description: Inspect the undersides of leaves for small green caterpillars (cabbage worms) and clusters of aphids. Remove by hand or use insecticidal soap.

careTasks.name: Harvest main head
careTasks.description: Harvest the main head when it is firm and tight, with densely packed green buds. Cut the stalk at an angle, leaving the plant to produce side shoots.

careTasks.name: Harvest side shoots
careTasks.description: After harvesting the main head, continue to harvest smaller side shoots every 5-7 days to encourage continuous production.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Broccoli needs consistent moisture to produce large heads. Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Water at the base of the plant to keep the heads dry and prevent rot.

name: Cabbage
description: A cool-season crop that forms dense heads of tightly packed leaves. Comes in green, red, and savoy varieties.
tips: Provide consistent moisture to prevent heads from splitting. Rotate crops to avoid soil-borne diseases.
succession: For a continuous harvest, plant new seedlings every 2-3 weeks, choosing varieties with different maturity dates.
yield: One primary head per plant; some varieties may produce smaller secondary heads.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when the head is firm and has reached a desirable size. Cut the stem at the base of the plant. Leaving the stalk and roots may encourage small secondary heads to form.
containerGardening: Compact varieties can be grown in 5-10 gallon containers. Requires consistent moisture to prevent heads from splitting.

soil.notes: Rich in organic matter. Sensitive to nutrient deficiencies, especially nitrogen.

temperature.notes: Can tolerate light frost, which can sweeten the flavor. Excessive heat can cause bolting.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cabbage is frost tolerant and flavor improves with a light frost. Cover only if a severe freeze is expected.

storage: Store in a cool, moist place like a root cellar or refrigerator for several months. Excellent for making sauerkraut or kimchi for long-term preservation.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply mulch to maintain even soil moisture and suppress weeds.

careTasks.name: Monitor for cabbage worms and slugs
careTasks.description: Inspect leaves for small green caterpillars and signs of slugs. Use row covers or hand-pick pests.

careTasks.name: Harvest when head is firm
careTasks.description: Harvest cabbage when the head is firm to the touch and has reached a desirable size. Cut the stem at the base of the plant.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Consistent watering is crucial for cabbage to form dense heads and prevent them from splitting. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry.

name: Cauliflower
description: A cool-season crop that requires steady, cool temperatures to form a dense head of flower buds.
tips: Cauliflower is more sensitive to temperature changes than its cabbage-family relatives. Avoid disturbing roots when transplanting.
succession: Succession planting is possible but challenging due to its sensitivity to temperature. Best to focus on a spring and fall crop.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when the head is 6-8 inches in diameter, firm, and the curds are still smooth. If it starts to look 'ricey' (curds separating), harvest immediately. Cut the entire head off the plant.
containerGardening: Challenging but possible in large (5-10 gallon) pots. Very sensitive to inconsistent watering and temperature swings.

soil.notes: Requires consistent supply of nutrients, especially boron, to prevent hollow stems. Side-dress with compost mid-season.

temperature.notes: Very sensitive to temperature swings. Protect from both frost and heat to prevent 'buttoning' (forming tiny heads).

environmentalAlerts.message: Cauliflower is sensitive to frost. Cover plants to protect developing heads.

storage: Store wrapped in plastic in the fridge for 1-2 weeks. Can be blanched and frozen or pickled.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Blanch the head
careTasks.description: When the head is 2-3 inches in diameter, tie the outer leaves over it to protect it from the sun and keep it white. Some varieties are self-blanching.

careTasks.name: Check for harvest readiness
careTasks.description: Harvest when the head is 6-8 inches in diameter, firm, and the curds are still smooth. If it starts to look 'ricey', harvest immediately.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Cauliflower is fussy and needs consistent moisture to form a single, large head. Water when the top inch of soil is dry, especially as the head develops.

name: Brussels Sprouts
description: A long-season, cool-weather crop where edible sprouts form in the leaf axils along a tall, central stem.
tips: A light frost improves the sprouts' flavor, making them sweeter. Provide support or staking in windy areas.
succession: Not typically succession planted due to its long growing season. Plant once for a late fall/early winter harvest.
yield: 50-100 sprouts per plant, harvested over several weeks.
harvestInstructions: Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upwards when they are firm, green, and 1-2 inches in diameter. Twist or snap them off. Flavor improves after a light frost.
containerGardening: Possible in large, deep pots (10+ gallons) with staking for support. A long-season commitment.

soil.notes: Benefits from soil amended with compost and a balanced fertilizer. Needs firm soil to anchor its tall stalk.

temperature.notes: Requires a long, cool growing season. Hot weather can cause sprouts to be bitter or loose.

environmentalAlerts.message: Brussels Sprouts are very frost tolerant and flavor improves with frost. No action needed for light frost.

storage: Refrigerate loose sprouts for a few weeks. Storing the entire stalk in a cool place keeps them fresh longer. Can be blanched and frozen.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Remove lower leaves
careTasks.description: As sprouts begin to form, remove the lower 6-8 leaves to direct energy into sprout development and improve air circulation.

careTasks.name: Top the plant (optional)
careTasks.description: About a month before harvest, you can cut off the top growing point of the plant to encourage all sprouts to mature at once.

careTasks.name: Begin harvesting bottom sprouts
careTasks.description: Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upwards when they are firm, green, and 1-2 inches in diameter. Twist or snap them off.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Consistent moisture is needed for a good harvest of Brussels sprouts. Water when the top 1-2 inches of soil feel dry.

name: Leeks
plantingDepth: 1/2 inch deep in flats, or in 6-inch deep trenches in the garden.
description: A member of the onion family with a mild, sweet flavor, grown for its thick, white edible stem.
tips: Plant in trenches and gradually fill in soil to blanch the stems (keep them white and tender).
succession: Can be succession planted every 2-3 weeks for a continuous harvest from late summer through winter.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when stalks are about 1 inch in diameter. Loosen the soil with a fork and gently pull them up. Can be harvested from late summer through early winter.
containerGardening: Can be grown in deep pots (at least 12 inches). Hilling is achieved by adding more soil to the pot as they grow.

soil.notes: Prefers sandy or loamy soil. They are heavy feeders and benefit from compost-rich soil.

temperature.notes: Very cold-hardy and can be harvested even after the ground freezes lightly. Flavor improves with cool weather.

environmentalAlerts.message: Leeks are very cold hardy. No action needed for frost.

storage: Store in the fridge for 2-4 weeks. Can also be left in the ground and harvested as needed in mild climates. Can be chopped and frozen.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Hill soil around stems to blanch
careTasks.description: Gradually mound soil up around the stems every few weeks. This keeps the lower portion from turning green, resulting in a more tender, flavorful leek.

careTasks.name: Fertilize mid-season
careTasks.description: Side-dress with compost or a balanced liquid fertilizer to support their long growing season.

careTasks.name: Begin harvesting mature leeks
careTasks.description: Harvest leeks when they are about 1 inch in diameter. Loosen the soil with a fork and gently pull them up.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Leeks need consistent moisture for long, tender stems. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry.

name: Asparagus
plantingDepth: Plant 1-year-old crowns in a 6-8 inch deep trench, with crowns 18 inches apart.
description: A perennial vegetable that, once established, will produce tender spears for up to 20 years. Requires patience.
tips: Plant 1-year-old crowns for a faster harvest. Avoid harvesting any spears in the first year to allow strong root systems to develop.
succession: Not applicable; it is a perennial that produces for many years from the same root system.
yield: 0.5-1 lb of spears per plant per season, once established.
harvestInstructions: Do not harvest the first year. In the second year, harvest for 2-3 weeks. From year 3 on, harvest all spears that are pencil-thick or larger for 6-8 weeks by snapping them off at the base.
containerGardening: Not recommended. Asparagus is a long-term perennial that requires a large, permanent bed to establish its extensive root system.

soil.notes: Requires deep, fertile soil free of weeds. Prepare the planting bed thoroughly as it is a long-term commitment.

temperature.notes: Emerging spears are sensitive to hard frost. The plant goes dormant in winter and requires a chilling period.

environmentalAlerts.message: Emerging asparagus spears are sensitive to frost. Cover the bed if frost is expected during harvest time.

storage: Best eaten fresh. Store spears upright in a glass with an inch of water in the fridge for up to a week. Can be blanched and frozen.

careTasks.name: Do not harvest (Year 1)
careTasks.description: Allow all spears to grow into ferns. This feeds the root system and builds energy for future years. Keep the bed well-weeded.

careTasks.name: Fertilize in early spring
careTasks.description: Apply a balanced fertilizer or top-dress with compost each spring before spears emerge.

careTasks.name: Begin light harvest (Year 2)
careTasks.description: You can harvest a few spears per plant for 2-3 weeks. Stop when spear diameter decreases significantly.

careTasks.name: Full harvest season (Year 3+)
careTasks.description: Harvest all spears that are pencil-thick or larger for 6-8 weeks. Stop harvesting when ferns begin to open.

careTasks.name: Cut back dead ferns in fall
careTasks.description: After the ferns have turned yellow or brown in the fall, cut them back to the ground to prevent disease.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Asparagus needs deep watering to establish a strong perennial root system. Water when the top 1-2 inches of soil are dry during the growing season. It is fairly drought-tolerant once established.

name: Fennel (Bulbing)
description: A cool-season crop grown for its swollen, licorice-flavored stem base, known as a bulb.
tips: Consistent watering is crucial; dry soil can cause the plant to bolt (flower prematurely) instead of forming a bulb.
succession: Sow every 2-3 weeks for a continuous harvest in cool weather. Avoid planting in the heat of summer.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when the bulb is firm and about the size of a tennis ball. Cut the plant off at the soil line. The fronds can be used as an herb.
containerGardening: Grows well in pots that are at least 10 inches deep to accommodate the taproot. Requires consistent watering to prevent bolting.

soil.notes: Amend soil with compost before planting. Does not compete well with weeds.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop. Hot weather or a sudden drop in temperature will cause it to bolt before a bulb forms.

environmentalAlerts.message: Fennel can be sensitive to frost. Cover plants to protect from frost damage.

storage: Store in a plastic bag in the fridge crisper for up to a week. The flavor fades over time.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Hill soil around developing bulbs
careTasks.description: When the base of the stem begins to swell, mound soil up around it. This blanches the bulb, making it more tender and white.

careTasks.name: Harvest when bulb is tennis-ball size
careTasks.description: Harvest when the bulb is firm and about the size of a tennis ball. Cut the plant off at the soil line. Some may resprout smaller shoots.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Consistent moisture is critical for fennel to form a bulb instead of bolting. Water whenever the top inch of soil feels dry.

name: Artichoke
plantingDepth: 1/2 inch deep for seeds, or plant crowns with the top just at the soil surface.
description: A large, thistle-like perennial plant that produces edible flower buds. Can be grown as an annual in colder climates.
tips: Artichokes are heavy feeders and require ample space, water, and nutrients to thrive.
succession: Not applicable; grown as a perennial in warm climates or an annual in colder zones.
yield: 5-10 primary buds and several smaller secondary buds per plant.
harvestInstructions: Harvest the main, terminal bud when it is large, firm, and the bracts are still tightly closed. Cut the stem 1-2 inches below the bud. Smaller side buds will follow.
containerGardening: Requires a very large container (20+ gallons) and is only feasible for a single season in most climates. Heavy feeder and water user.

soil.notes: Amend soil generously with compost and manure before planting. They are heavy feeders.

temperature.notes: Requires a period of cool weather (vernalization, below 50°F) to trigger budding. Protect crowns from hard frost with heavy mulch.

environmentalAlerts.message: Protect artichoke crowns from hard frost with a heavy layer of mulch.

storage: Store in a plastic bag in the fridge for 1-2 weeks. Best when cooked soon after harvesting. The hearts can be preserved in oil or marinated.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply a thick layer of mulch to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and keep roots cool.

careTasks.name: Fertilize regularly
careTasks.description: Feed with a balanced liquid fertilizer every 3-4 weeks during the growing season.

careTasks.name: Harvest main bud
careTasks.description: Harvest the main, terminal bud when it is large, firm, and the bracts (scales) are still tightly closed. Cut the stem about 1-2 inches below the bud.

careTasks.name: Harvest side buds
careTasks.description: After the main bud is cut, the plant will produce smaller side buds. Harvest these when they reach a usable size.

careTasks.name: Winterize the plant (perennials)
careTasks.description: In the fall, cut the entire plant back to about 6 inches and cover the crown with a thick layer of mulch to protect it from frost.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Artichokes are thirsty plants that need regular, deep watering to produce large, tender buds. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, especially as the buds form.
